## Rationale

Input resistance (Rin) is a core intrinsic property that sets the gain and time course of synaptic integration. Across adult mouse visual cortex GABAergic interneurons, Rin spans a >5-fold range: parvalbumin (PV) basket cells are low (~50–150 MΩ), somatostatin (SST) Martinotti cells intermediate (~150–300 MΩ), and VIP/Id2 interneurons high (~200–500 MΩ). Because Rin is essentially the reciprocal of the total resting membrane conductance (plus a geometric term from membrane area), explaining Rin variation requires identifying the channels that carry the resting "leak" conductance in these cells. Patch-seq—paired whole-cell recording and single-cell transcriptomics from the same neuron—provides a direct, cell-by-cell way to test candidate channel genes.

The resting conductance of central neurons is dominated by constitutively open K⁺ "leak" channels of the two-pore-domain (K2P) family. Among these, TASK-1 (KCNK3) and TASK-3 (KCNK9) are the best-characterized neuronal background K⁺ channels: they heterodimerize, are open at rest, are K⁺-selective, and are modulated by extracellular pH, PIP₂, and Gq-coupled neuromodulators. They are expressed in cortex, including in GABAergic interneurons (Talley et al., 2001; Enyedi & Czirják, 2010). Genetic deletion of TASK-3 increases input resistance and excitability in cerebellar granule cells (Brickley et al., 2007), establishing that graded TASK channel activity can set Rin. Their transcript levels vary across and within interneuron transcriptomic types, making them prime candidates for Patch-seq-based mechanistic dissection.

## Hypothesis

In adult mouse visual cortex GABAergic interneurons, cell-to-cell variation in input resistance is primarily determined by graded expression of the TASK-1/TASK-3 (KCNK3/KCNK9) heteromeric leak K⁺ conductance: cells with higher KCNK3 + KCNK9 transcript levels have a larger standing K⁺ conductance, a more negative resting membrane potential, and a lower input resistance. In particular, PV cells (lowest Rin) are predicted to express the highest levels of KCNK3/KCNK9, whereas Id2/VIP cells (highest Rin) express the lowest.

## Test

1. In existing Patch-seq datasets (e.g., mouse visual cortex; Gouwens et al., 2020; Scala et al., 2021), regress Rin (or resting conductance, 1/Rin) on KCNK3 and KCNK9 expression, controlling for transcriptomic type, membrane area/morphology, and other conductances (HCN1, KCNJ2, KCNQ2/3). The hypothesis predicts a negative partial correlation.
2. Pharmacological test: apply TASK blockers (e.g., ML365, bupivacaine, doxapram) or TASK activators to identified interneurons and measure the change in Rin; the effect should scale with KCNK3/KCNK9 expression.
3. Genetic test: Kcnk3/Kcnk9 knockout or knockdown in identified interneuron types should increase Rin and depolarize RMP, with the largest effect in cells with the highest baseline expression.
4. Validate transcript–protein correspondence with single-cell RT-PCR or smFISH for KCNK3/KCNK9 in recorded cells.

## Caveats

Membrane area and other resting conductances (HCN, Kir, KCNQ, tonic GABA_A) also contribute; space-clamp and series-resistance errors can distort Rin; and TASK channels are modulated by pH/PIP₂, so cell state may matter.

## Conclusion

The general principle—that K⁺ leak channels set neuronal Rin—is established (Brickley et al., 2007; Enyedi & Czirják, 2010). The specific claim that graded TASK-1/TASK-3 expression explains cell-to-cell Rin variation among cortical GABAergic interneurons is a new, directly testable mechanism that Patch-seq is ideally suited to address.
